claims.text: The nominal Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 refractory high-entropy alloy forms a single BCC solid solution.
The NbTaTiV alloy can be produced by arc melting followed by high-temperature homogenization.
Random elemental distributions produce substantial or severe lattice distortion in the alloy.
Lattice distortion modifies predominantly edge-dislocation core configurations.
Lattice distortion displaces edge-dislocation cores from their neutral planes and produces wavy dislocation lines.
Wavy edge-dislocation configurations impede dislocation mobility at lower temperatures.
Increasing temperature enables atomic motion to partially overcome the effects of lattice distortion.
Partial thermal overcoming of lattice distortion changes dislocation dynamics and increases elastic anisotropy.
The alloy exhibits temperature-dependent changes in dislocation behavior.
Compressive testing and in situ neutron diffraction can be performed on NbTaTiV from room temperature through 900°C.
Resonant ultrasound spectroscopy is to be applied across the full room-temperature-to-900°C range.
The controlled compression tests use a strain rate of 1 × 10^-4 s^-1.
The NbTaTiV alloy retains a single BCC phase up to 900°C.
At room temperature, the alloy has low elastic anisotropy, with a Zener anisotropy ratio of approximately 1.2.
At room temperature, the alloy has high yield strength.
Limited dislocation mobility caused by lattice distortion is responsible for the high room-temperature yield strength.
At 900°C, the Zener anisotropy ratio approaches 1.6.
The yield strength decreases as temperature rises from room temperature to 900°C.
The elevated-temperature yield strength is reduced relative to conventional BCC-alloy baselines.
Conventional BCC alloys show higher temperature sensitivity in elastic anisotropy and are typically governed by screw dislocations.

contradictions.description: The mechanism places wavy dislocation configurations at lower temperature and predicts that increasing temperature partially overcomes distortion, whereas the falsification rule refers to a transition to wavy configurations without specifying that it should occur at low temperature. This makes the expected direction of the proposed dislocation-core transition internally ambiguous.
